lessons.title: Divide Multi-Digit Numbers Using an Algorithm
lessons.objective: I can divide multi-digit whole numbers and explain the meaning of the quotient and remainder.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my division using the words dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder.

concept.heading: How do you divide big numbers?
concept.intro: Dividing means splitting a total into equal groups. Long division finds the quotient one digit at a time by repeating the same four steps: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
concept.keyIdea: Algorithm: A step-by-step set of rules or instructions to solve a math problem. Long Division Algorithm: D (Divide), M (Multiply), S (Subtract), B (Bring Down). Formula: Divisor ) Dividend = Quotient R Remainder. 1. D - Divide: write quotient digit above the bar. 2. M - Multiply: digit × divisor. 3. S - Subtract: find the difference. 4. B - Bring down: next digit from dividend. 5. Repeat: continue until no digits remain (leftover = remainder). Example: 1,344 ÷ 12 = 112

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I want 1,344 ÷ 12. The dividend is 1,344 and the divisor is 12, so 12 goes outside the bracket and 1,344 goes inside.
DIVIDE: 12 does not fit into 1, so I look at 13. How many 12s fit into 13? One. I write 1 above the 3.
MULTIPLY: 1 × 12 = 12. I write 12 underneath the 13.
SUBTRACT: 13 − 12 = 1. That is what is left so far.
BRING DOWN: I bring the next digit, 4, down next to the 1 to make 14. Now I repeat the cycle.
REPEAT: 14 ÷ 12 → 1 (written above the 4), 1 × 12 = 12, 14 − 12 = 2, and I bring down the last 4 to make 24.
REPEAT: 24 ÷ 12 → 2 (written above the last 4), 2 × 12 = 24, 24 − 24 = 0. Nothing is left to bring down, so the remainder is 0.
The digits I wrote are 1, 1, 2, so 1,344 ÷ 12 = 112. I check by multiplying: 12 × 112 = 1,344.
linesEs: Quiero 1,344 ÷ 12. El dividendo es 1,344 y el divisor es 12, así que el 12 va fuera de la galera y 1,344 va adentro.
Divide: el 12 no cabe en 1, así que miro 13. ¿Cuántos 12 caben en 13? Uno. Escribo 1 arriba del 3.
Multiplica: 1 × 12 = 12. Escribo 12 debajo del 13.
Resta: 13 − 12 = 1. Eso es lo que queda por ahora.
Baja: bajo el siguiente dígito, el 4, junto al 1 para formar 14. Ahora repito el ciclo.
Repite: 14 ÷ 12 → 1 (escrito arriba del 4), 1 × 12 = 12, 14 − 12 = 2, y bajo el último 4 para formar 24.
Repite: 24 ÷ 12 → 2 (escrito arriba del último 4), 2 × 12 = 24, 24 − 24 = 0. No queda nada por bajar, así que el residuo es 0.
Los dígitos que escribí son 1, 1, 2, así que 1,344 ÷ 12 = 112. Lo compruebo multiplicando: 12 × 112 = 1,344.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's do 384 ÷ 8. DIVIDE: 8 does not fit into 3, so we look at 38. How many 8s fit into 38? (4 — write it above the 8.)
MULTIPLY: what is 4 × 8? (32 — write it under the 38.)
SUBTRACT: what is 38 − 32? (6.)
BRING DOWN: bring the 4 down next to the 6. What number do you have now? (64.)
DIVIDE: how many 8s fit into 64? (8 — write it above the 4.)
MULTIPLY: what is 8 × 8? (64 — write it under the 64.)
SUBTRACT: what is 64 − 64? (0.)
BRING DOWN: is there another digit left to bring down? (No — the remainder is 0, so 384 ÷ 8 = 48. Check: 8 × 48 = 384.)
linesEs: Hagamos 384 ÷ 8. Divide: el 8 no cabe en 3, así que miramos 38. ¿Cuántos 8 caben en 38? (4 — escríbelo arriba del 8.)
Multiplica: ¿cuánto es 4 × 8? (32 — escríbelo debajo del 38.)
Resta: ¿cuánto es 38 − 32? (6.)
Baja: baja el 4 junto al 6. ¿Qué número tienes ahora? (64.)
Divide: ¿cuántos 8 caben en 64? (8 — escríbelo arriba del 4.)
Multiplica: ¿cuánto es 8 × 8? (64 — escríbelo debajo del 64.)
Resta: ¿cuánto es 64 − 64? (0.)
Baja: ¿queda otro dígito para bajar? (No, el residuo es 0, así que 384 ÷ 8 = 48. Comprueba: 8 × 48 = 384.)

vocabulary.definition: A step-by-step set of rules or instructions to solve a math problem.
The total number being divided into equal groups (the number inside the division bracket).
vocabulary.example: In 1,344 ÷ 12 = 112, the dividend is 1,344 — the total amount being divided

vocabulary.definition: The number of equal groups you are dividing into (the number outside the division bracket).
vocabulary.example: In 1,344 ÷ 12 = 112, the divisor is 12 — the number of equal groups

vocabulary.definition: The answer when you divide.
vocabulary.example: In 156 ÷ 12 = 13, the quotient is 13 — there are 13 groups

vocabulary.definition: What is left over when a number does not divide evenly.
vocabulary.example: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 R 2 means 3 groups of 5 with 2 left over

vocabulary.definition: Separate a multi-digit number into equal groups to find a quotient.
A method that repeats four steps — divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — until there are no digits left to bring down.
vocabulary.example: 1,344 ÷ 12 → divide, multiply, subtract, bring down, repeat

vocabulary.definition: The fourth step of long division: move the next digit of the dividend down next to what is left, then start the cycle again.
vocabulary.example: 13 − 12 = 1, then bring down the 4 to make 14

lessons.title: Divide Decimals Using an Algorithm
lessons.objective: I can divide with decimals by making the divisor a whole number first.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words dividend, divisor, quotient, and equivalent division.

concept.heading: How do you divide with decimals?
concept.intro: Dividing splits a total into equal groups. When you divide by a decimal, first move the point to make the divisor a whole number — then run the same long-division cycle: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.
concept.keyIdea: Decimal Division Algorithm. 1. Make the divisor a whole number: slide its decimal point to the right. 2. Slide the dividend's decimal point to the right the same number of places. 3. Write the answer's decimal point in the column directly above the dividend's point, then divide as whole numbers using Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring Down.

worked.title: Watch me
lines: I want 18.9 ÷ 6.3. The divisor is 6.3, and long division needs a whole-number divisor.
STEP 0 — MOVE THE POINT: I move the decimal point 1 place right in the divisor, so 6.3 becomes 63.
I slide the decimal point 1 place to the right in the dividend too, so 18.9 becomes 189. Both points slid the same 1 place, so the answer does not change. The problem is now 189 ÷ 63.

Now I write it the tall way — 63 into 189 — with the answer going on top of the bar and the answer's decimal point in the column directly above the dividend's point. Then I repeat the same four steps I always use: DIVIDE, MULTIPLY, SUBTRACT, BRING DOWN.
DIVIDE: 63 does not fit into 1 or 18, so my first working number is 189. How many 63s fit into 189? Three. I write 3 above the 9.
MULTIPLY: 3 × 63 = 189. I write it underneath.
SUBTRACT: 189 − 189 = 0.
BRING DOWN: there are no digits left to bring down, so the cycle is finished and the remainder is 0. 18.9 ÷ 6.3 = 3.
I check by multiplying: 6.3 × 3 = 18.9. Correct — 18.9 ÷ 6.3 = 3.
linesEs: Quiero 18.9 ÷ 6.3. El divisor es 6.3, y la división larga necesita un divisor entero.
Paso 0 — mueve el punto: muevo el punto decimal 1 lugar a la derecha en el divisor, así que 6.3 se convierte en 63.

Deslizo el punto decimal 1 lugar a la derecha en el dividendo también, así que 18.9 se convierte en 189. Los dos puntos se deslizaron el mismo lugar, así que la respuesta no cambia. El problema ahora es 189 ÷ 63.

Ahora lo escribo en vertical — 189 entre 63 — con la respuesta arriba de la línea y el punto decimal de la respuesta en la columna justo arriba del punto del dividendo. Luego repito los mismos cuatro pasos de siempre: divide, multiplica, resta, baja.
Divide: el 63 no cabe en 1 ni en 18, así que mi primer número de trabajo es 189. ¿Cuántos 63 caben en 189? Tres. Escribo 3 arriba del 9.
Multiplica: 3 × 63 = 189. Lo escribo debajo.
Baja: no quedan dígitos por bajar, así que el ciclo termina y el residuo es 0. 18.9 ÷ 6.3 = 3.
Lo compruebo multiplicando: 6.3 × 3 = 18.9. Correcto — se pueden llenar 3 cápsulas.

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's do 8.4 ÷ 2.1. STEP 0 — MOVE THE POINT: how many places make 2.1 a whole number? (1 place, so 2.1 becomes 21.)
Now slide the decimal point 1 place to the right in the dividend too. What does 8.4 become? (84, so the new problem is 84 ÷ 21.)
DIVIDE: how many 21s fit into 84? (Four. I write 4 on top, above the 4 in 84.)
MULTIPLY: what is 4 × 21? (84. I write it underneath the 84.)
SUBTRACT: what is 84 − 84? (0.)
BRING DOWN: is there another digit left to bring down? (No — nothing is left, so 8.4 ÷ 2.1 = 4. Check: 2.1 × 4 = 8.4.)
linesEs: Hagamos 8.4 ÷ 2.1. Paso 0 — mueve el punto: ¿cuántos lugares hacen que 2.1 sea un número entero? (1 lugar, así que 2.1 se convierte en 21.)
Ahora desliza el punto decimal 1 lugar a la derecha en el dividendo también. ¿En qué se convierte 8.4? (En 84, así que el nuevo problema es 84 ÷ 21.)
Divide: ¿cuántos 21 caben en 84? (Cuatro. Escribo 4 arriba, sobre el 4 de 84.)
Multiplica: ¿cuánto es 4 × 21? (84. Lo escribo debajo del 84.)
Resta: ¿cuánto es 84 − 84? (0.)
Baja: ¿queda otro dígito para bajar? (No, no queda nada, así que 8.4 ÷ 2.1 = 4. Comprueba: 2.1 × 4 = 8.4.)

vocabulary.definition: The number of equal groups you are dividing into (the number outside the division bracket).

feedback: 12 × 68 = 816, which lands short of 936. Check the tens digit of your quotient before you bring down the next number.
That is close: 12 × 76 = 912, which is 24 away from 936. Multiply your quotient back by 12 each time to see whether it lands exactly on the dividend.
87 reverses the digits of the quotient — and 87 × 12 = 1,044, which is more than 936. Redo the long division and keep each digit in its correct place.
hints: Estimate first: 12 × 70 = 840 and 12 × 80 = 960, so the quotient must land between 70 and 80.
Set it up as long division and DIVIDE first — how many 12s fit into 93?
DIVIDE: 93 ÷ 12 → 7. MULTIPLY: 7 × 12 = 84. SUBTRACT: 93 − 84 = 9. BRING DOWN the 6 to make 96, then repeat the cycle.

support.explanation: 5 × 497 = 2,485. Running the cycle: 24 ÷ 5 → 4 with 4 left, 48 ÷ 5 → 9 with 3 left, 35 ÷ 5 → 7 with 0 left, so the quotient is 497 and the remainder is 0.
feedback: 487 × 5 = 2,435, which is 50 short of 2,485 — a ten was lost in the middle of the division. Redo it and check each digit as you bring the next one down.
You are very close, but 5 × 496 = 2,480 and 5 are still left over. A leftover that big means the ones digit is not finished yet.
A zero slipped into the tens place: 5 × 507 = 2,535, which is more than 2,485. Recheck what is left after you divide the hundreds.
hints: Size it up: 5 × 500 = 2,500, just a bit more than 2,485 — so the quotient is a little under 500.
Set it up as long division and DIVIDE first — how many 5s fit into 24?
DIVIDE: 24 ÷ 5 → 4. MULTIPLY: 4 × 5 = 20. SUBTRACT: 24 − 20 = 4. BRING DOWN the 8 to make 48, then repeat until the last digit is used.

support.explanation: 9 × 84 = 756. Running the cycle: 75 ÷ 9 → 8 with 3 left, then 36 ÷ 9 → 4 with 0 left, so the quotient is 84 and the remainder is 0.
feedback: 83 × 9 = 747, which leaves 9 left over — a remainder as big as the divisor means the quotient is too small. Raise the ones digit by one and multiply to check.
9 × 86 = 774, a little past 756. Nudge the ones digit down and multiply back to test it.
9 × 94 = 846, which overshoots 756. Recheck the tens digit by asking how many 9s fit into 75.
hints: Anchor on a fact you know: 9 × 80 = 720, which is close to 756 — so the quotient is just above 80.
Set it up as long division and DIVIDE first — how many 9s fit into 75?
DIVIDE: 75 ÷ 9 → 8. MULTIPLY: 8 × 9 = 72. SUBTRACT: 75 − 72 = 3. BRING DOWN the 6 to make 36, then repeat the cycle.

support.explanation: 9 × 125 = 1,125. Running the cycle: 11 ÷ 9 → 1 with 2 left, 22 ÷ 9 → 2 with 4 left, 45 ÷ 9 → 5 with 0 left, so the quotient is 125.
feedback: 9 × 115 = 1,035 — that falls short of the dividend, so a ten went missing somewhere in the steps.
So close: 9 × 124 = 1,116, and another 9 still fits. Multiply back every time to see whether you land exactly on the dividend.
9 × 135 = 1,215, which is past 1,125. Recheck the tens digit by asking how many 9s fit into 22.
hints: Estimate first: 9 × 100 = 900 and 9 × 200 = 1,800, so the quotient lands between 100 and 200.
Set it up as long division and DIVIDE first — how many 9s fit into 11?
DIVIDE: 11 ÷ 9 → 1. MULTIPLY: 1 × 9 = 9. SUBTRACT: 11 − 9 = 2. BRING DOWN the 2 to make 22, then repeat until the last digit is used.

steps: Problem: Divide 1,134 ÷ 9 with long division. Dividend = 1,134, divisor = 9.
Divide, Multiply, Subtract: 9 does not fit into 1, so start with 11. 11 ÷ 9 → 1. 1 × 9 = 9, and 11 − 9 = 2
Bring down, repeat: Bring down the 3 to make 23. 23 ÷ 9 → 2. 2 × 9 = 18, and 23 − 18 = 5
Final answer: Quotient = 12, remainder = 5
support.explanation: The student stopped one cycle early: the 4 at the end of 1,134 was never brought down. Bring it down next to the 5 to make 54, then DIVIDE 54 ÷ 9 → 6, MULTIPLY 6 × 9 = 54, SUBTRACT 54 − 54 = 0. The quotient is 126 with remainder 0, and 9 × 126 = 1,134 checks it.
hints: Count the digits of 1,134 that have been used so far. Is one of them still waiting to be brought down?
Bring the last digit down next to the leftover 5, run one more divide–multiply–subtract cycle, then check with 9 × quotient.

feedback: The decimal point slid in the wrong direction. Since 1.2 fits into 14.4 more than once, the quotient has to be greater than 1.
Check: 1.2 × 1.2 is only 1.44, not 14.4 — the decimal slid one place too far. Multiply both numbers by 10 so the problem becomes 144 ÷ 12.
That result is 10 times too large — a sign the decimal point moved in only one of the numbers. Scale the dividend and the divisor by the same power of 10.
hints: Dividing by a decimal is awkward — notice the divisor 1.2 has one decimal place. There's a move that makes it whole.
Multiply BOTH numbers by 10: scaling dividend and divisor the same way keeps the quotient exactly the same.
Compute 14.4 × 10 = 144 and 1.2 × 10 = 12. Now solve 144 ÷ 12 — a whole-number division you already know how to do.

feedback: The digits are right, but the decimal point moved two places the wrong way. Dividing by a number less than 1 gives a quotient larger than the number you started with.
Your digits are right, but the decimal point is one place too far left. Since 0.6 is less than 1, the quotient must be greater than 3.78.
63 × 0.6 = 37.8, ten times too big — the decimal point moved one place too far right. After multiplying both numbers by 10, you divide 37.8 by 6, so the quotient keeps a decimal.
hints: The divisor 0.6 has one decimal place — shifting both numbers one place makes the divisor a whole number.
Multiply both numbers by 10 to build an equivalent problem, then divide, keeping the decimal point in the dividend.
3.78 × 10 = 37.8 and 0.6 × 10 = 6. Now compute 37.8 ÷ 6, keeping the decimal point lined up in your answer.

feedback: The decimal point went the wrong way. 0.7 fits into 8.4 many times, so the quotient is much larger than 1.
Check: 1.2 × 0.7 is only 0.84, not 8.4 — the answer is ten times too small. Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 84 ÷ 7, then divide.
You multiplied 8.4 by 10 but left 0.7 alone. Both numbers have to grow by the same factor for the quotient to stay the same.
hints: Ask yourself: how many groups of 0.7 fit inside 8.4? Since 0.7 is less than 1, expect MORE groups than 8.
Scale both numbers by 10 so you're dividing by a whole number instead of a decimal.
8.4 becomes 84 and 0.7 becomes 7. Solve 84 ÷ 7 — your 7s times-table facts will carry you there.

feedback: Check: 1.2 × 1.3 is only 1.56, not 15.6 — the decimal shifted a place too far. Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 156 ÷ 13, then divide.
13 is the divisor after scaling, not the quotient. You still have to divide 156 by 13.
This result is 10 times too large. Check that you multiplied both 15.6 and 1.3 by the same power of 10 before dividing.
hints: The divisor 1.3 isn't a whole number — shift both numbers before you divide anything.
Multiply dividend and divisor by 10, then divide. Check at the end: your answer times 1.3 should rebuild 15.6.
15.6 × 10 = 156 and 1.3 × 10 = 13. Now count how many 13s fit into 156 — start by trying 13 × 10.

steps: Problem: Solve 6.4 ÷ 0.8.
Move the divisor's decimal: 0.8 becomes 8 (moved 1 place right).
Divide without moving the dividend: 6.4 ÷ 8 = 0.8
support.explanation: The student moved the decimal point in the divisor (0.8 → 8) but forgot to move it the same 1 place in the dividend. You must move BOTH: 6.4 becomes 64, so 64 ÷ 8 = 8. So 6.4 ÷ 0.8 = 8. Check: 8 × 0.8 = 6.4. ✓
hints: When you moved 0.8 to 8, what did you have to do to 6.4 as well?
Move the decimal the same 1 place in both: 6.4 → 64, then 64 ÷ 8 = 8.

core.prompt: A warehouse has 2,184 items to pack into boxes of 14. How many boxes are needed?
feedback: 146 boxes × 14 = 2,044 items, which leaves 140 items unpacked. Multiply your answer by 14 and check that it rebuilds exactly 2,184.
14 × 155 = 2,170, which leaves 14 items with no box. Multiply back to test whether your quotient uses up every item.
14 × 166 = 2,324, which is more items than the warehouse actually has. Check the tens digit of your quotient.
hints: The question asks how many groups of 14 fit into 2,184 — that phrase 'how many boxes' signals division.
Estimate to anchor yourself: 14 × 150 = 2,100 is close to 2,184. Then set it up as long division and run the cycle.
DIVIDE: 21 ÷ 14 → 1. MULTIPLY: 1 × 14 = 14. SUBTRACT: 21 − 14 = 7. BRING DOWN the 8 to make 78, then repeat the cycle.

steps: Problem: Divide 2,058 ÷ 14 with long division. Dividend = 2,058, divisor = 14.
Divide, Multiply, Subtract: 14 does not fit into 2, so start with 20. 20 ÷ 14 → 1. 1 × 14 = 14, and 20 − 14 = 6
Bring down, repeat: Bring down the 5 to make 65. 65 ÷ 14 → 4. 4 × 14 = 56, and 65 − 56 = 9
Bring down, repeat: Bring down the 8 to make 98. 98 ÷ 14 → 8. 8 × 14 = 112, and 98 − 112 = −14
Final answer: Quotient = 148
core.explanation: The DIVIDE step in the last cycle chose a digit that is too big: 8 × 14 = 112 is more than the 98 you have to subtract from, and you can never subtract more than the working number. The right digit is 7, since 7 × 14 = 98 and 98 − 98 = 0. The quotient is 147 with remainder 0, and 14 × 147 = 2,058 rebuilds the dividend.
hints: Look at the last cycle. After you MULTIPLY, the product has to be small enough to SUBTRACT from 98. Is 112?
A negative difference means the DIVIDE step picked too large a digit. Try the largest digit whose product with 14 still fits inside 98, then finish the cycle.

core.prompt: A water tank holds 19.2 liters. It is poured into bottles that each hold 1.6 liters. How many bottles can be filled?
feedback: The digits look right—how many total decimal places should the product have?
Check the division: make the divisor a whole number by moving both decimals one place (192 ÷ 16), then divide.
That is one bottle more than the division gives. Multiply both numbers by 10 and divide 192 by 16 carefully — it comes out even, with nothing left over.
hints: You're asking how many 1.6s fit into 19.2 — that's division, and the divisor 1.6 needs to become whole first.
Multiply both amounts by 10 to build an equivalent whole-number division, then divide.
19.2 × 10 = 192 and 1.6 × 10 = 16. Now run the cycle on 192 ÷ 16: DIVIDE 19 ÷ 16 → 1, MULTIPLY 1 × 16 = 16, SUBTRACT 19 − 16 = 3, BRING DOWN the 2.

steps: Problem: Solve 9.6 ÷ 0.12.
Count how far to move: 0.12 has 2 decimal places, so BOTH numbers move 2 places right. The divisor: 0.12 → 12.
Move the dividend the same 2 places: 9.6 only has one digit after the point, so the student moved it just 1 place: 9.6 → 96. New problem: 96 ÷ 12 = 8.
core.explanation: Both numbers must move the SAME number of places — 2, not 1. 9.6 runs out of digits after one place, so you add a placeholder zero to move the second place: 9.6 → 96 → 960. The real problem is 960 ÷ 12 = 80, so 9.6 ÷ 0.12 = 80. Estimate to confirm: 0.12 is tiny, so many of them fit in 9.6 — the quotient must be large, not 8. Check: 80 × 0.12 = 9.6. ✓
hints: The divisor moved 2 places (0.12 → 12), so the dividend has to move 2 places too — the student only moved it 1.
9.6 has no second digit to move, so add a placeholder zero: 9.6 → 960. Then 960 ÷ 12 = 80.

steps: Problem: 1,536 ÷ 16
Divide: 16 does not fit into 1 or 15, so start with 153. 153 ÷ 16 → 9, written above the 3
Multiply: 9 × 16 = 144, written under the 153
Subtract: 153 − 144 = 19
Bring down: Bring down the 6 to make 196
Final answer: Quotient = 9 with 196 left over
stretch.explanation: The SUBTRACT step is wrong: 153 − 144 = 9, not 19. Long division has a built-in warning here — the difference after you subtract must always be SMALLER than the divisor, and 19 is bigger than 16. With the correct difference of 9, bring down the 6 to make 96, then DIVIDE 96 ÷ 16 → 6 and SUBTRACT 96 − 96 = 0. The quotient is 96 with remainder 0, and 16 × 96 = 1,536.
hints: After you SUBTRACT, compare the difference to the divisor. What should always be true about a difference of 19 when the divisor is 16?
Redo the subtraction 153 − 144 carefully, bring down the 6, and finish the cycle. Then test the result with 16 × quotient.

stretch.prompt: The station must load 3,360 ration packs equally into 14 storage pods. Solve it with long division. Name each step — divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — and check your answer by multiplying.
stretch.frame: 3,360 ÷ 14 = ___. I divided ___ by 14 and wrote ___ , then multiplied, subtracted and brought down the next digit each time. I checked by multiplying: 14 × ___ = 3,360.
stretch.explanation: Long division on 3,360 ÷ 14 runs the cycle three times: 33 ÷ 14 → 2 (2 × 14 = 28, leaving 5), bring down the 6 → 56 ÷ 14 → 4 (4 × 14 = 56, leaving 0), bring down the 0 → 0 ÷ 14 → 0, so a 0 must be written in the ones place. The quotient is 240 ration packs per pod, and 14 × 240 = 3,360 proves none were left over.
hints: Re-read the sentence frame: it wants the four named steps — divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — not just the answer.
Set it up as 14 into 3,360. Since 14 does not fit into 3, your first working number is 33.
DIVIDE: 33 ÷ 14 → 2. MULTIPLY: 2 × 14 = 28. SUBTRACT: 33 − 28 = 5. BRING DOWN the 6 to make 56, then repeat — and watch what you must write when you bring down the final 0.

steps: Problem: 7.2 ÷ 0.45
Multiply divisor by 10: 0.45 × 10 = 4.5
Multiply dividend by 10: 7.2 × 10 = 72
stretch.explanation: Derek only multiplied by 10, but the divisor 0.45 has two decimal places. He should multiply both numbers by 100: 720 ÷ 45 = 16. He got the right answer by luck this time, but his method is unreliable because the divisor is still a decimal (4.5).
hints: How many decimal places does 0.45 have? Did Derek multiply by enough to make it a whole number?
0.45 has two decimal places, so multiply both by 100, not 10. 0.45 × 100 = 45 and 7.2 × 100 = 720.

stretch.prompt: A gas station sells fuel at $3.45 per gallon. A customer pays $27.60 total. How many gallons did the customer buy? Set up the decimal division, show how to convert it to whole-number division, and solve.
stretch.frame: The equation is $27.60 ÷ $3.45 = ___. I multiply both by ___ to get ___ ÷ ___ = ___ gallons.
stretch.explanation: Total cost divided by price per gallon gives the number of gallons, so the setup is 27.60 ÷ 3.45. The divisor has two decimal places, so multiplying both numbers by 100 gives 2,760 ÷ 345 = 8 gallons, and 8 × $3.45 = $27.60 confirms it.
hints: Total money ÷ price per gallon = gallons, so set up 27.60 ÷ 3.45 — and notice the divisor has TWO decimal places.
Multiply both numbers by 100 so the divisor becomes a whole number, then divide the two new whole numbers.
27.60 × 100 = 2,760 and 3.45 × 100 = 345. Now ask how many 345s fit into 2,760 — note that 345 × 10 = 3,450 is already too big.
